St. Matrona of Moscow

Saints

St. Matrona of Moscow

Matronushka · St. Matrona Nikonova

Period
1881–1952 in the official life
Region
Russia
Titles / vocation
Woman · Lay
Commemoration
April 19/May 2 (paired calendars in the official life)

Introduction

St. Matrona Nikonova is the blind Russian laywoman commemorated by the OCA for her prayerful care of visitors and the suffering.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Repose in 1952; not an execution narrative.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The OCA describes a poor family in Sebino, Tula province, blindness from birth, and loss of the use of her legs as a teenager.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 1; Published biographical account,paragraph 2; Published biographical account,paragraph 3

Father Edward Pehanich places Matrona in a poor rural family and recounts a visit to St. John of Kronstadt at fourteen. His article gives a different birth year from the OCA life; the entry therefore retains the official life’s 1881 rather than pretending all sources agree.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 4; The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 6

Pehanich describes a child who learned services by memory in the village church near her home. His narrative follows gratitude from visitors who brought food for the family, and later dependence on friends. These details portray a laywoman without formal schooling rather than a founder of a monastery or theological school.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 4; The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 7; The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 9; The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 13

Life and notable events

She moves to Moscow in 1925. The life describes repeated moves under atheist persecution and many visitors seeking her prayers and counsel.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 2

Pehanich’s account describes her brothers’ Communist affiliations and their anxiety about visitors seeking religious help. It follows her dependence on friends in Moscow and movement between apartments. It portrays her receiving distressed visitors, offering consolation, and insisting that healing came from God. Its reported foresight and healing are the priest’s published hagiographic account, not independently established medical claims.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 7; The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 9; The Blind Saint With Sight,body,paragraph 17

The life places her homes among believers who sheltered her and describes the visitors’ needs as both bodily and spiritual. It reports preserved testimonies of healing and foreknowledge as part of her veneration. Her inability to see or walk is thus a concrete part of this published life, alongside its account of active care for others.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 1; Published biographical account,paragraph 2

Death and martyrdom

She dies in 1952 and is buried in Danilov cemetery. The selected account does not report execution or martyrdom.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 3; Published biographical account,paragraph 4

Writings and legacy

The official life records local glorification in 1999 and her relics at Moscow’s Protection Convent; additional diocesan history is attributed below.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 3

The Moscow Patriarchate’s May 2000 synodal report records approval of an akathist to locally venerated Righteous Matrona. This is a dated institutional record of her reception, not a new prayer composed for this app.

[3] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 9; Published biographical account,paragraph 11; Published biographical account,paragraph 15

Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms.

Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:

And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him.

Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.

Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months.

And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth her fruit.

Father Pehanich’s Matrona article explicitly cites James5: 16. This passage supplies the surrounding biblical context, not a newly composed prayer or visitor rule.

[4] Public-domain Bible translation · James 5: 13–18
